_meta.description: Fixed ground truth evaluation set for the Grounded Enterprise Policy & Procedure Assistant (PE6201). Locked BEFORE the RAG system was implemented or evaluated, to avoid tuning test cases to match RAG output.
_meta.corpus_version: 16-document synthetic SynthCorp procurement policy corpus (15 policy files/, files 01-16 -- file 16 added as a superseded/outdated policy version; see amendment note)
_meta.note: Superseded by the amendment below. Kept for history: the original 20-case set omitted a 'conflicting/outdated policy' category because the corpus contained no versioned or contradictory content to draw from -- simulating one only inside a test question, without the underlying documents actually containing it, would have meant inventing procurement rules rather than testing against the corpus.

amendment.reason: Reviewer feedback on the Problem Statement: an evaluation corpus the team wrote itself should actually contain a superseded policy version and a genuine cross-document contradiction, not only simulate them in test questions.
amendment.corpus_change: Added 15 policy files/16_provincial_trade_policy_2019_superseded.txt (a 2019 edition of the Provincial Trade Policy, explicitly labelled SUPERSEDED, that states a different, no-longer-effective rule than the current 12_provincial_trade_policy.txt). Added a 'CURRENT EDITION' cross-reference paragraph to 12_provincial_trade_policy.txt. Added a 'GIFT ACCEPTANCE GUIDANCE' paragraph to 14_procurement_governance_roles.txt that directly contradicts the absolute gift ban in 13_conflict_of_interest_policy.txt, and says so in its own text.
amendment.ground_truth_change: Added TC21 and TC22 (category 'conflicting_or_outdated_policy'), raising num_cases from 20 to 22.
amendment.reproducibility_note: Because the corpus changed, the calibration set (evaluation/calibration/calibration_questions.json), the frozen thresholds (rag/thresholds.py), and every downstream result file were regenerated by re-running the existing, unmodified pipeline scripts in the existing order (see README section 11). No scoring rule, threshold-selection rule, or evaluation script was changed to produce a particular outcome -- only the mechanical re-run was needed. TC01-TC20 and their expected values are unchanged.
amendment.not_test_set_tuning: TC21/TC22 were authored before re-running retrieval/calibration on the changed corpus, from the documents' own content, not from observing the RAG system's output on them.

test_cases.question: How many supplier quotations are required for a $100,000 goods purchase?
test_cases.expected_answer: A minimum of three (3) supplier quotations must be obtained, using the standard goods Invitation to Quote (ITQ) template.
test_cases.explanation: A $100,000 goods purchase falls cleanly inside the $75,000-$121,199.99 tier with no boundary ambiguity, and only one document is needed to answer it.

test_cases.question: Who approves a $50,000 consulting engagement?
test_cases.expected_answer: Approval is given by the requesting Department Manager.
test_cases.explanation: $50,000 falls inside the below-$75,000 consulting tier, and the source document gives this exact dollar figure as a worked example, so this is a direct lookup.

test_cases.question: What is the SynthCorp Procurement Card per-transaction limit?
test_cases.explanation: A single, unambiguous fact stated once in one document.

test_cases.question: What must be attached to a Purchase Order when it is created?
test_cases.expected_answer: All supplier quotations that were received must be attached, regardless of whether that supplier was selected, including any 'no quotation' responses from invited suppliers who did not quote.
test_cases.explanation: Direct procedural fact from a single document, no threshold or ambiguity involved.

test_cases.question: How does a supplier become an Approved Supplier?
test_cases.expected_answer: A prospective supplier applies through the SynthCorp Supplier Portal to Central Procurement Services, submitting business registration information, relevant compliance documentation, and at least one business reference. Central Procurement Services reviews the application and adds qualifying suppliers to the Approved Supplier list.
test_cases.explanation: Direct procedural description from a single document.

test_cases.question: What procurement process applies to a goods purchase of exactly $75,000?
test_cases.expected_answer: A $75,000 goods purchase falls into Tier 3 ($75,000 to $121,199.99): a minimum of three (3) supplier quotations are required using the goods ITQ template, approval is given by the Director, and the resulting Purchase Order must be reviewed by the Contracting Authority.
test_cases.explanation: Tests the exact $74,999.99/$75,000 boundary between Tier 2 and Tier 3; a system that misclassifies the boundary inclusively/exclusively will fail this case.

test_cases.question: What procurement process applies to a goods purchase of $74,999?
test_cases.expected_answer: A $74,999 goods purchase falls into Tier 2 ($25,000 to $74,999.99): a minimum of two (2) supplier quotations are required, and approval is given by the Department Head.
test_cases.explanation: Mirror-image boundary case to TC06, one dollar below the Tier 2/Tier 3 line.

test_cases.question: What procurement process applies to a goods purchase of exactly $121,200?
test_cases.expected_answer: A $121,200 goods purchase falls into Tier 4 ($121,200 or more): an open competitive procurement process (formal tender or Request for Proposal) is required, and approval must be given by the Contracting Authority, in consultation with Central Procurement Services.
test_cases.explanation: Tests the exact $121,199.99/$121,200 boundary between Tier 3 and Tier 4.

test_cases.question: Is a Procurement Policy Exemption Justification (PPEJ) required for a non-competitive purchase of exactly $25,000?
test_cases.expected_answer: No. The PPEJ requirement is triggered only when the total procurement value exceeds $25,000. A value of exactly $25,000 does not exceed the threshold, so this specific PPEJ rule is not triggered at exactly $25,000.
test_cases.explanation: Tests precise wording ('exceeds $25,000') against a superficial misreading that $25,000 itself would trigger the rule; a strict-inequality boundary case.

test_cases.question: Does a non-competitive consulting engagement of exactly $1,000,000 require additional Vice President or Executive Procurement Committee approval?
test_cases.expected_answer: Yes. A non-competitive consulting engagement of $1,000,000 or more requires additional, higher-level approval from a Vice President or the Executive Procurement Committee, in addition to the standard PPEJ process.
test_cases.explanation: Tests that 'or more' is inclusive of exactly $1,000,000, distinguishing the below-$1,000,000 and $1,000,000-or-more tiers.

test_cases.question: What procurement method applies to a purchase of $75,000?
test_cases.explanation: The question does not specify goods or services, and the two tracks genuinely diverge at $75,000: goods = Tier 3 (3 quotes, Director + Contracting Authority review), services = Tier 2 (2 quotes, Director only). The correct behaviour is to ask which type of purchase this is, not to guess.

test_cases.question: Who approves a $50,000 purchase?
test_cases.explanation: Goods approval at $50,000 is the Department Head; services approval at $50,000 is the Department Manager. These are different roles, so the question must be clarified rather than answered with one guess.

test_cases.question: How many quotes are required for a $90,000 purchase?
test_cases.explanation: Goods at $90,000 require 3 quotes; services at $90,000 require 2 quotes. The dollar figure alone does not determine the answer.

test_cases.question: How many quotes are required for a $10,000 purchase?
test_cases.explanation: Goods below $25,000 require no formal quotations; services below $75,000 require a minimum of one. The two rules disagree at $10,000, so goods-vs-services must be clarified.

test_cases.question: What is the approval requirement for a $30,000 purchase?
test_cases.explanation: Goods approval at $30,000 is the Department Head; services approval at $30,000 is the Department Manager. Answering without knowing the purchase type would be a guess.

test_cases.question: What disciplinary action applies to an employee who violates this procurement policy?
test_cases.explanation: The corpus addresses consequences for non-compliant suppliers (removal from the Approved Supplier list) and audit exposure for improper exemptions, but never states any disciplinary process for an employee. No document supports an answer.

test_cases.question: Can an unsuccessful supplier appeal a procurement decision, and what is the appeal process?
test_cases.explanation: No document describes any supplier appeal or dispute mechanism. This is a plausible procurement topic that is simply absent from the corpus.

test_cases.question: What insurance or liability coverage must a supplier carry to bid on SynthCorp contracts?
test_cases.explanation: The supplier-fairness and Approved Supplier documents describe registration and conduct expectations but never mention insurance or liability coverage requirements.

test_cases.question: How long must procurement records be retained before they can be destroyed?
test_cases.explanation: The documentation and governance documents require records to be 'retrievable for audit or review purposes' but never state a specific retention period or destruction rule. A plausible near-miss: retrieval may surface record-keeping chunks that sound relevant but do not actually answer the question.

test_cases.question: What currency or exchange-rate rules apply when purchasing from a supplier outside Canada and the United States?
test_cases.explanation: The provincial trade policy document addresses Ontario-based preference and US-supplier restrictions only. It never addresses other countries or currency/exchange-rate handling.

test_cases.question: What is the Ontario supplier preference under the provincial trade policy?
test_cases.expected_answer: The current Provincial Trade Policy gives a regional preference to Ontario-based suppliers, where all else (such as price and quality) is comparable, but only for purchases below $121,200. A 2019 edition of this document also exists in the policy files; it applied the preference to all purchases with no dollar limit, but that 2019 edition is explicitly labelled SUPERSEDED and must not be used for a current procurement decision.
test_cases.explanation: Two versions of the Provincial Trade Policy exist in the corpus: the current edition (12_provincial_trade_policy.txt), which caps the Ontario preference at purchases below $121,200, and a 2019 edition (16_provincial_trade_policy_2019_superseded.txt), explicitly marked SUPERSEDED, that applied the preference with no dollar limit. Lexical (TF-IDF) retrieval can rank the superseded document above the current one, since it repeats the phrase 'Ontario preference' more directly -- this case tests whether the system uses the document's own SUPERSEDED label, not retrieval rank, to decide which version is authoritative.

test_cases.question: Can an employee accept a gift from a supplier?
test_cases.expected_answer: The corpus contains two unreconciled rules on this question. The Conflicts of Interest in Procurement document (13_conflict_of_interest_policy.txt) states that procurement participants must not accept gifts or favours from current or prospective suppliers. The Procurement Governance Roles document (14_procurement_governance_roles.txt) states that gifts of nominal value (under $50) may be accepted if disclosed to the Department Manager, and explicitly notes this has not been reconciled with the conflict-of-interest rule. A correct answer must surface this conflict rather than silently follow only one rule, and recommend confirming with the policy owner.
test_cases.explanation: 13_conflict_of_interest_policy.txt and 14_procurement_governance_roles.txt state directly conflicting gift-acceptance rules for the same situation, and 14_procurement_governance_roles.txt explicitly says the two have not been reconciled. This exercises the system's ability to detect and surface a genuine cross-document policy contradiction rather than confidently answering with only one side of it.
